sentence: Skin cancer is not a single disease.
note: NHS has separate melanoma and non-melanoma pages.

sentence: The NHS describes two broad groups, melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, and gives each its own information.
The two main types of non-melanoma skin cancer are basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
note: Summary: two main types BCC and SCC.

sentence: The NHS says basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer in the UK, with squamous cell carcinoma the second most common.
Ultraviolet (UV) light is the main cause of both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, and it comes from sunlight and from sunbeds.
note: NHS: UV main/most common cause; NHS Shropshire: sunlight and sunbeds.

sentence: Surgery is the main treatment for both groups, particularly when the cancer is found early.
note: NHS: surgery main treatment, especially if found early.

sentence: For non-melanoma skin cancer, the NHS says that finding it early makes it easier to treat.
note: Summary: early detection makes it easier to treat.

sentence: Because skin cancers can look different from one another, the pages that follow describe the melanoma and non-melanoma signs separately, followed by causes, tests and treatment.
note: Structural sentence reflecting that sources describe the two groups separately.

sentence: The NHS describes a new mole, or a change in an existing mole, as the main sign of melanoma.
A mole that changes in size, shape or colour may be a melanoma.
Other warning signs include a mole that is swollen, sore, bleeding, itchy or crusty.
Cancer Research UK points out that some melanomas cause no symptoms at all and that most do not cause pain or itching.
note: Summary: some melanomas don't cause symptoms; most don't give pain or itching.

sentence: A checklist called ABCDE is often used to describe the features to look for, standing for asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolving.
note: Summary: ABCDE letters; sources differ on diameter.

sentence: Cancer Research UK notes that a melanoma can be small when it is diagnosed early.
note: Summary: can be smaller if diagnosed early.

sentence: In people with brown or black skin, melanoma can be harder to spot and may appear on the palms, the soles of the feet or under a nail.
note: Summary: harder to spot, palms, soles, under nail.

sentence: Such a melanoma might not show the usual ABCD signs, or might be broken and sore (ulcerated).
The NHS says the main symptom of non-melanoma skin cancer is a growth or unusual patch on the skin.
These growths and patches can vary in colour, size and texture.
The NHS lists a growth that is getting bigger, has changed colour or texture, or that hurts, itches, bleeds, crusts or scabs for more than four weeks.
It advises seeing a GP about changes of this kind.
The NHS also advises seeing a GP about a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks.
note: NHS melanoma page wording in summary.

sentence: A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet describes actinic keratoses as patches linked to sun-damaged skin.
It says people who have them are more at risk of all types of skin cancer than people of the same age who do not.
The leaflet also says to examine the skin every few months and to seek a review if a patch changes.
The NHS names ultraviolet (UV) light as the main cause of melanoma and the most common cause of non-melanoma skin cancer.
The risk comes from sunlight and from sunbeds.
Pale skin, a large number of moles and a family history of skin cancer increase the risk of melanoma.
Cancer Research UK also lists older age, and having a close relative who has had melanoma.
For non-melanoma skin cancer, the risk is higher in people who have had one before or who have a family history of skin cancer.
Sun protection lowers the risk, according to the sources, and the British Association of Dermatologists leaflet advises avoiding sunlamps and sunbeds because they give out UV light.
note: NHS: sun protection lowers risk; BAD leaflet.

sentence: The US National Cancer Institute notes that sunscreen prevents sunburn, but that it may encourage more sun exposure in fair-skinned people at risk, so sunscreen is one measure among several.
note: Summary of NCI prevention text (US source). The last clause is a paraphrase, not stated verbatim.

sentence: A GP can examine the skin and may refer the person to a dermatologist if unsure.
If a GP suspects melanoma, the NHS says the person is referred to a hospital specialist and should get an appointment within two weeks.
The usual test is an excision biopsy, in which the specialist may cut out the mole and a small area of surrounding skin.
The sample is sent to a laboratory and checked for cancer.
For non-melanoma skin cancer, the diagnosis is usually confirmed by cutting out a section of affected skin and checking it for cancer.
If melanoma is found, further scans or blood tests may follow to work out how far it has spread.
MedlinePlus says that melanoma which is very deep, or has spread to the lymph nodes, is more likely to return after treatment.
The NHS says surgery is the main treatment for melanoma, especially if it is found early.
Radiotherapy, targeted medicines, immunotherapy and chemotherapy are used for more advanced melanoma, and their use depends on the stage and location of the cancer.
Surgery is also the main treatment for non-melanoma skin cancer, particularly when it is found early.
The choice of treatment depends on the type and the location of the cancer.
Other options include radiotherapy, creams applied to the skin and photodynamic therapy.
note: Summary; NHS Shropshire page lists creams and PDT.

sentence: Mohs surgery is a specialist technique in which the surgeon removes the cancer in thin layers.
A paper summarising UK guidance reports that it is reserved for cancers affecting critical structures, cancers that have come back, and basal cell carcinomas of more aggressive subtypes.
note: Summary: UK guidance reports reserved for these cases (PMC paper, not an official page).

sentence: They are two broad groups of skin cancer that the NHS describes on separate pages.
The main non-melanoma types are basal cell carcinoma, which is the most common skin cancer in the UK, and squamous cell carcinoma.
Both groups are mainly caused by ultraviolet light, and surgery is the main treatment for both, especially when found early.
Ultraviolet light from the sun or from sunbeds is named by the NHS as the main cause of skin cancer.
A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet advises avoiding sunlamps and sunbeds because they give out UV light.
The same leaflet says protecting the skin from the sun may reduce the risk of sun-induced skin cancer.
Cancer Research UK says that some melanomas cause no symptoms and that most do not cause pain or itching.
The NHS lists pain, itching, bleeding and crusting among the changes in a mole or growth that are worth a GP visit.
The signs therefore vary between people and between types of skin cancer.
The NHS and Cancer Research UK list pale skin, a large number of moles and a family history of skin cancer as increasing the risk of melanoma.
The NHS says people who have had a non-melanoma skin cancer before are also at higher risk of another.
A British Association of Dermatologists leaflet says people with actinic keratoses are more at risk of all types of skin cancer.
The NHS says the person is referred to a specialist in hospital and should get an appointment within two weeks.
The specialist may remove the mole and a small area of surrounding skin, which is sent to a laboratory to be checked for cancer.
Further scans or blood tests may follow if cancer is found, to see how far it has spread.
The NHS says surgery is the main treatment, especially when the cancer is found early.
The choice depends on the type and location of the cancer.
Radiotherapy, creams applied to the skin and photodynamic therapy are other options that are sometimes used.
